title: The Proton-Motive Force and ATP Synthase

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: On an oxygen-electrode record of isolated mitochondria with fuel, respiration with ADP present is called {{c1::State 3}}.
cards.back: State 4 is respiration after the ADP has been used up; the slope flattens again.
cards.quote: Add a little ADP and the slope steepens at once: State 3, respiration with ADP.

cards.front: About how much energy is the proton-motive force (Δp) worth per mole of protons crossing the inner mitochondrial membrane?
cards.back: About 19 kJ per mole of protons.
cards.quote: Every proton that crosses the inner membrane is priced by one shared number, the proton-motive force Δp, worth about 19 kJ per mole of protons.

cards.front: In mitochondria, how do the proton pumps and ATP synthase each respond as Δp rises, and where does Δp settle?
cards.back: The pumps earn Δp and push against it, so they slow as it rises. ATP synthase and any leak spend it and speed up. Δp settles where earning equals spending.
cards.quote: The pumps earn Δp and must push against it, so they slow as it rises.

cards.front: In Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, what stores the energy that links electron flow to ATP synthesis?
cards.back: A proton gradient across a sealed membrane, not a high-energy chemical intermediate.
cards.quote: stored not in a high-energy chemical intermediate but in a proton gradient across a sealed membrane
cards.section: How we know: a gradient alone makes ATP

cards.front: Chloroplast membranes are soaked in acid, then jumped into base, with no light and no electron transport (Jagendorf and Uribe). What happened, and what does it show?
cards.back: They made ATP in the dark. A hand-built proton gradient alone is enough to drive ATP synthase.
cards.quote: a hand-built proton gradient, with no light and no electron transport. They made ATP in the dark.
cards.section: How we know: a gradient alone makes ATP

cards.front: Racker and Stoeckenius built vesicles from purified lipids, bacteriorhodopsin and ATP synthase only, then shone light on them. What was the result, and what does it show?
cards.back: ATP appeared with no respiratory chain anywhere. The light-driven pump built a gradient, and the gradient alone drove the synthase.
cards.quote: Shine light, and the pump builds a gradient, the gradient drives the synthase, and ATP appears, with no respiratory chain anywhere.
cards.section: How we know: a gradient alone makes ATP

cards.front: Lit vesicles containing bacteriorhodopsin and ATP synthase are making ATP. An uncoupler that carries protons straight back across the membrane is added; the light stays on. What happens to ATP synthesis, and why?
cards.back: It stops, or nearly. The pump still earns, but the leak spends faster than the pump can rebuild, so the gradient collapses and the synthase has nothing to spend.
cards.why: Pump and synthase share nothing but the gradient.
cards.quote: The pump still earns, but the leak spends faster than the pump can rebuild, so the gradient collapses and the synthase has nothing to spend.
cards.section: How we know: a gradient alone makes ATP

cards.front: Chloroplast membranes are given an acid-to-base jump as in the acid-bath experiment, but an uncoupler is present in the bath. Predict ATP synthesis, and explain.
cards.back: Little or no ATP. The pH difference alone can bias the rotor, but the uncoupler carries the protons back across the membrane, so the gradient drains without passing through the synthase.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the gradient is the only link, and a leak spends it without making ATP.
cards.quote: The voltage and the pH difference both supply that bias, which is why the acid-bath chloroplasts could turn theirs with a pH jump alone.
cards.section: A motor, not a metaphor

cards.front: The membrane potential ΔΨ leaves the mitochondrial matrix about {{c1::150 mV}} negative, which pulls positive protons back in.
cards.back: This is the electrical part of Δp.
cards.quote: leaving the matrix about 150 mV negative, which attracts the positive protons back
cards.section: What the dam stores: Δp, in one number

cards.front: At body temperature, a one-unit pH difference (tenfold in concentration) pushes protons as hard as about {{c1::61.5 mV}}.
cards.back: This converts ΔpH into millivolts so it can be added to ΔΨ.
cards.quote: a tenfold concentration difference, exactly one pH unit, pushes as hard as 61.5 mV (log scales)
cards.section: What the dam stores: Δp, in one number

cards.front: A mitochondrion has ΔΨ = 150 mV and ΔpH = 0.75. Calculate Δp, the electrical share, and the energy per mole of protons (F = 96.5 kJ per mole per volt).
cards.back: Chemical part: 61.5 × 0.75 = 46 mV. Δp = 150 + 46 = 196 mV. Electrical share: 150/196, about three-quarters. Energy: 96.5 × 0.196 = 18.9 kJ/mol.
cards.quote: Take ΔΨ = 150 mV and ΔpH = 0.75. Chemical part: 61.5 × 0.75 = 46 mV.
cards.section: What the dam stores: Δp, in one number

cards.front: A mitochondrion is treated so the pH is equal on both sides of its inner membrane, but its membrane potential rises to 180 mV. Can it still make ATP?
cards.back: Yes. Δp = 180 + 61.5 × 0 = 180 mV, about 17 kJ per mole of protons, at the low end of the usual range.
cards.why: The synthase responds to the total pull. Tracking only pH would wrongly predict no ATP.
cards.quote: Δp = 180 + 61.5 × 0 = 180 mV, about 17 kJ per mole of protons, at the low end of the usual range.
cards.section: What the dam stores: Δp, in one number

cards.front: Mitochondria have ΔΨ = 140 mV and ΔpH = 0.5. Using Δp = ΔΨ + 61.5 mV × ΔpH, find Δp and the energy per mole of protons (F = 96.5 kJ per mole per volt).
cards.back: Chemical part: 61.5 × 0.5 = 30.75 mV. Δp = 140 + 30.75 ≈ 171 mV. Energy: 96.5 × 0.171 ≈ 16.5 kJ/mol. The electrical term is about 82% of the total.
cards.quote: Add them and divide by F: Δp = ΔΨ + (2.303RT/F) × ΔpH.
cards.section: What the dam stores: Δp, in one number

cards.front: Why must at least about three protons fall through ATP synthase for each ATP delivered to the cytosol?
cards.back: Making and delivering ATP costs about 50 to 60 kJ/mol in a working cell, and each proton is worth about 19 kJ/mol: 55 / 19 is about 3.
cards.why: The cost exceeds the 30.5 kJ/mol standard value because the cell keeps ATP high and ADP low.
cards.quote: 55 / 19 is about 3, so at least about three protons must fall per ATP delivered.
cards.section: One price for every proton

cards.front: ATP synthase spends about 3.7 protons per exported ATP, not the bare minimum of about 3. Why does that margin matter?
cards.back: The margin keeps the synthase running forward. A machine spending exactly the minimum would sit at equilibrium and make nothing.
cards.quote: That margin keeps it running forward; a machine spending exactly the minimum would sit at equilibrium and make nothing.
cards.section: One price for every proton

cards.front: The respiratory chain pumps about ten protons per NADH, and NADH-to-oxygen electron transfer releases about 220 kJ/mol at standard potentials. At Δp = 200 mV, what do the ten protons cost, and what margin is left?
cards.back: Per proton: 96.5 × 0.200 = 19.3 kJ/mol. Ten protons: 193 kJ, about 88% of 220. Margin: about 27 kJ at standard potentials.
cards.quote: At Δp = 200 mV those ten protons cost 10 × 19.3 = 193 kJ, about 88% of the standard total.
cards.section: One price for every proton

cards.front: What happens to electron flow through the respiratory chain if Δp climbs to about 220 mV, and what is this effect called?
cards.back: The pumps' energy margin is gone, so electron flow slows to a trickle. This is back-pressure.
cards.quote: if Δp climbs to about 220 mV, the margin is gone and electron flow slows to a trickle
cards.section: One price for every proton

cards.front: Name the main parts of ATP synthase and where each sits.
cards.back: Fo, in the membrane: a ring of c-subunits (rotor) against a stationary a-subunit with two offset half-channels. F1, in the matrix: α3β3 head around a bent γ shaft bolted to the c-ring.
cards.quote: F o sits in the membrane: a ring of c-subunits (the rotor) pressed against a stationary a-subunit that holds two offset half-channels.
cards.section: A motor, not a metaphor

cards.front: In the Fo rotor of ATP synthase, why can only a c-subunit carrying a proton rotate away from the a-subunit into the lipid?
cards.back: A charged group cannot sit in the oily core of the membrane. Protonating the c-subunit's acidic residue neutralizes it, so it can enter the lipid.
cards.quote: A charged group cannot sit in the oily core of the membrane; only a c-subunit whose acid carries a proton can turn away from the a-subunit into the lipid.
cards.section: A motor, not a metaphor

cards.front: In Boyer's binding-change mechanism, name the three states each β subunit of ATP synthase cycles through, and what happens in each.
cards.back: Open: releases finished ATP, takes in ADP and Pi. Loose: holds ADP and Pi loosely. Tight: ATP forms spontaneously and is held firmly.
cards.quote: Each β subunit cycles through three states as γ turns: Open (releases finished ATP, takes in ADP and Pi)
cards.section: Boyer's inside-out insight: where the energy goes

cards.front: In ATP synthase, each 120° turn of γ releases one ATP, so a full turn releases {{c1::three}} ATP.
cards.quote: Each 120° turn of γ moves all three forward one state and releases one ATP, so a full turn releases three.
cards.section: Boyer's inside-out insight: where the energy goes

cards.front: In the binding-change mechanism of ATP synthase, what does the energy of the proton gradient mainly pay for?
cards.back: Above all, prying the finished ATP loose from the Tight site, and also driving the binding of ADP and Pi. Making the bond on the enzyme costs almost nothing.
cards.quote: On the enzyme, making the bond costs almost nothing either way.
cards.section: Boyer's inside-out insight: where the energy goes

cards.front: The F1 head of ATP synthase is detached from the membrane, so there is no Fo and no gradient, and given ATP. What does it do, and what does this say about the gradient's role?
cards.back: It hydrolyzes ATP, and γ spins the opposite way from synthesis. The gradient does not make the chemistry possible; it sets the direction.
cards.quote: The gradient does not make the chemistry possible; it sets the direction.
cards.section: Boyer's inside-out insight: where the energy goes

cards.front: ATP-fed α3β3γ heads were fixed to glass with a fluorescent actin filament attached to γ (Noji and Yoshida). What did the filament do, and what does it show?
cards.back: It spun in discrete 120° steps, one per ATP. ATP synthase is a real rotary motor, with one catalytic event per third of a turn.
cards.quote: spun an attached fluorescent actin filament in discrete 120° steps, one per ATP
cards.section: Boyer's inside-out insight: where the energy goes

cards.front: The vertebrate ATP synthase c-ring has 8 subunits. How many protons per ATP does rotation alone cost?
cards.back: Eight protons and three ATP per turn: 8 / 3 ≈ 2.7 H⁺ per ATP.
cards.quote: Eight protons and three ATP per turn: 8 / 3 ≈ 2.7 H⁺ per ATP.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: Why does each ATP exported from the mitochondrion cost about 3.7 H⁺ rather than the 2.7 used by the c8 rotor?
cards.back: The ATP–ADP translocase swaps ATP⁴⁻ out for ADP³⁻ in, so ΔΨ moves one net negative charge outward, and the phosphate carrier imports Pi with a proton. Together: about one more proton-equivalent.
cards.quote: Together, the two carriers cost about one more proton-equivalent, for about 3.7 H⁺ per exported ATP, just above the floor of about three.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: Why is cytosolic NADH worth about 1.5 ATP via the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle but about 2.5 ATP via the malate-aspartate shuttle?
cards.back: The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle hands electrons to FAD and CoQ, bypassing Complex I's pumping. The malate-aspartate shuttle regenerates matrix NADH, which enters at Complex I.
cards.quote: The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle delivers them to FAD and CoQ, bypassing Complex I, so that NADH is worth only about 1.5 ATP.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: Two cytosolic NADH enter mitochondria by the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle instead of the malate-aspartate shuttle. Using exam values, how many fewer ATP are made?
cards.back: Malate-aspartate: 2 × 2.5 = 5 ATP. Glycerol-3-phosphate: 2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP. Difference: 2 ATP.
cards.why: This is one reason the per-glucose yield is quoted as a range, about 30–32.
cards.quote: The malate-aspartate shuttle regenerates matrix NADH, worth about 2.5 ATP.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: Why is the yield of about 30–32 ATP per glucose only approximate?
cards.back: The shuttle mix varies with tissue, enzyme levels and metabolic state; the proton cost per exported ATP is not a whole number; and proton leak and slip lower measured yields.
cards.quote: Many tissues run both, and the mix depends on enzyme levels and metabolic state.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: With 3.7 H⁺ per ATP, the c8 synthase would allow about 2.7 ATP per NADH, yet measured P/O ratios in isolated mitochondria come out near 2.5. Explain the gap.
cards.back: Proton leak and slip: some protons return to the matrix without making ATP, so part of the pumped gradient is spent with no ATP output.
cards.quote: Measured P/O ratios fall below the c8 ceiling mainly because of proton leak and slip: some protons return without making ATP.
cards.section: Shuttles and measured yields

cards.front: An engineered mitochondrion has 12 c-subunits instead of 8, with transport still costing about one extra proton per exported ATP and about ten protons pumped per NADH. Estimate ATP per NADH, compared with wild type.
cards.back: Rotor: 12 / 3 = 4 H⁺, plus 1 for transport = 5 H⁺ per ATP. 10 / 5 = 2 ATP per NADH, versus 10 / 3.7 ≈ 2.7 for c8. Less efficient.
cards.why: Rests on three ATP per turn, ten protons per NADH and about one proton-equivalent for export.
cards.quote: The vertebrate c-ring has 8 subunits, the smallest ring and lowest proton cost per ATP known.
cards.section: Counting protons and ATP

cards.front: A working cell's ATP costs about 55 kJ/mol to make and deliver. If ΔpH collapses to 0 while ΔΨ stays at 150 mV, can the synthase still make ATP at 3.7 H⁺ per ATP? (F = 96.5 kJ per mole per volt)
cards.back: Δp = 150 mV, so each proton is worth 96.5 × 0.15 ≈ 14.5 kJ/mol. 3.7 × 14.5 ≈ 53.6 kJ, below 55. Net synthesis stalls; about 3.8 protons would be needed just to break even.
cards.why: Rests on Δp = ΔΨ + 61.5 mV × ΔpH and the rule that a machine at the minimum sits at equilibrium.
cards.quote: Making ATP and delivering it to the cytosol costs about 50 to 60 kJ/mol in a working cell
cards.section: One price for every proton

cards.front: Resting mitochondria have fuel but almost no ADP. ADP is added. What happens first to Δp, then to the pumps, then to oxygen use?
cards.back: The synthase spends, so Δp dips. The pumps' margin grows, electrons flow faster and oxygen use rises (State 3). When ADP is used up, Δp climbs back and the chain idles (State 4).
cards.why: The chain feels ADP only through Δp.
cards.quote: ADP lets the synthase spend, so Δp dips.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Why can a small change in Δp produce a large change in electron flow through the respiratory chain?
cards.back: A 10 mV dip saves about 10 kJ on the ten protons pumped per NADH, widening the pumps' few-tens-of-kJ margin by a third or more.
cards.quote: A 10 mV dip in Δp saves about 10 kJ on the pumps' ten protons, widening their few-tens-of-kJ margin by a third or more.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Contrast how acceptor (respiratory) control and energy charge regulate ATP production.
cards.back: Acceptor control: ADP reaches the chain only through ATP synthase and Δp. Energy charge works upstream, telling enzymes such as PFK-1 how much fuel to send.
cards.quote: Energy charge, a gauge of the cell's balance of ATP, ADP and AMP, works upstream instead, telling enzymes such as PFK-1 how much fuel to send.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Energy charge, ([ATP] + ½[ADP]) / ([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]), is held near {{c1::0.85–0.90}}.
cards.back: It tunes PFK-1, isocitrate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: Energy charge, ([ATP] + ½[ADP]) / ([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]), is held near 0.85–0.90.
cards.section: Where energy charge fits

cards.front: Respiring mitochondria get oligomycin, then minutes later an uncoupler (DNP or FCCP). Predict O₂ consumption, ATP output and gradient size after each.
cards.back: Oligomycin: O₂ down to the leak rate, ATP down, gradient up. Then uncoupler: O₂ up, usually past the starting rate; gradient down; ATP still zero.
cards.why: Oligomycin removes spending through the synthase, so back-pressure slows the pumps. The uncoupler adds a large leak, opening the pumps' margin wide.
cards.quote: Oligomycin removes spending through the synthase. Δp rises as back-pressure, and the pumps slow until earning matches the small remaining leak.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Where in the respiratory chain do rotenone, antimycin A, and cyanide or CO act?
cards.back: Rotenone: Complex I. Antimycin A: Complex III. Cyanide or CO: Complex IV.
cards.quote: ETC inhibitors change the earning side: rotenone at Complex I, antimycin A at Complex III, cyanide or CO at Complex IV.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Isolated mitochondria respiring on pyruvate plus malate are given cyanide. Predict O₂ consumption, ATP output and gradient size.
cards.back: All three fall: O₂ down, ATP down, gradient down. Cyanide stops the earning side at Complex IV, so pumping stops.
cards.quote: Pumping stops: O₂ down, ATP down, gradient down.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Cold activates UCP1 in brown-fat mitochondria. Predict O₂ consumption, ATP output and the fate of the gradient's energy.
cards.back: O₂ rises while ATP output stays low. UCP1 leaks protons back into the matrix, bypassing ATP synthase, so the energy is released as heat (nonshivering thermogenesis).
cards.quote: UCP1 (thermogenin) in brown fat deliberately leaks protons to make heat instead of ATP
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: In ischemia, what can ATP synthase do once the chain stalls, and how does the IF1 protein respond?
cards.back: With the gradient collapsed, the synthase can run backward, burning ATP to hold Δp up. IF1 locks the rotor at low pH, stopping the reverse spin and saving ATP.
cards.quote: The IF1 inhibitor protein locks the rotor at low pH, stopping that reverse spin and saving the cell's ATP.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Cells lacking IF1 undergo ischemia. Compared with normal cells, predict what happens to their ATP during the oxygen shortage, and why.
cards.back: ATP falls faster. With the chain stalled and the gradient collapsed, the synthase can run backward, and without IF1 nothing locks the rotor, so it is expected to keep burning ATP to hold Δp up.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the synthase can reverse when the earning side stops, and that IF1 normally blocks that reverse spin.
cards.quote: In ischemia, when oxygen runs short, the chain stalls and the gradient collapses, so the synthase can run backward, burning ATP to hold Δp up.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: In a respirometry trace, baseline O₂ use falls after oligomycin, then rises above baseline after FCCP. Interpret the oligomycin drop, the oligomycin-resistant remainder, and the FCCP rise.
cards.back: The drop is O₂ use coupled to ATP synthesis. The remainder is the proton leak. The FCCP rise shows the chain was being held below its top rate by Δp back-pressure.
cards.why: Oligomycin removes synthase spending; an uncoupler adds a large leak, and the chain races to refill the gradient.
cards.quote: O₂ up, usually past the starting rate; gradient down; ATP still zero.
cards.section: Setting the rate, and breaking it on purpose

cards.front: Isolated mitochondria respiring on succinate are given rotenone. Predict O₂ consumption, ATP output and gradient size, and contrast with pyruvate plus malate as fuel.
cards.back: Pumping continues: succinate's electrons enter at Complex II, below the block, so Complexes III and IV keep pumping and the gauges do not collapse. With pyruvate plus malate, all three gauges fall.
cards.why: An ETC inhibitor stops pumping only for fuel that enters upstream of the block.
cards.quote: Rotenone blocks Complex I, but electrons from succinate still enter at Complex II.
cards.section: When blocking the chain does not empty the gradient

cards.front: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion becomes mildly leaky to protons while ADP supply is unchanged. Predict Δp, O₂ consumption and the ATP made per oxygen.
cards.back: Δp settles a little lower; the pumps' margin widens and O₂ use rises; more protons return without making ATP, so ATP per oxygen (P/O) falls.
cards.why: Rests on the earning-equals-spending rule: a leak is extra spending that makes no ATP.
cards.quote: To predict any drug, disease or change in demand, ask which side it changed (earning, spending through the synthase, or spending through a leak), then follow Δp to the other side.

cards.front: Brown-fat mitochondria with active UCP1 are given oligomycin. Predict O₂ consumption and ATP output, and explain.
cards.back: O₂ use falls from its peak but stays high, and ATP output stays low. Oligomycin removes only spending through the synthase; the UCP1 leak keeps spending Δp, so the pumps keep running.
cards.why: Rests on asking which side each agent changes and following Δp.
cards.quote: Δp settles where earning equals spending.
